articles.title: In Wyoming, AI cameras detected approaching eagles and slowed nearby turbines; a field study reported an 82% lower eagle-fatality rate than at a control wind farm
articles.summary: A field study in Wyoming demonstrated that AI technology effectively reduced eagle fatalities at wind farms by 82%, offering a promising solution for protecting wildlife while generating renewable energy.
articles.body: Wind turbines can kill eagles, and the usual remedy, curtailing turbines when an eagle is nearby, depends on someone spotting the bird in time. The conflict has long troubled both the wind industry and conservationists, because big raptors such as golden eagles fly along the same windy hills that make good turbine sites. Turning off turbines whenever an eagle might be in the area sounds simple until the question arises of who can see the bird in time.At Wyoming’s Top of the World wind farm, cameras and software now do that job. A device called IdentiFlight scans the skies, detects eagles and automatically curtails nearby turbines just before a possible collision. In January 2021, The Peregrine Fund, Western EcoSystems Technology and the US Geological Survey announced a study that found an eagle fatality rate 82% lower than at a reference wind farm.Why Top of the World needed a fixTop of the World and its neighbour Campbell Hill are wind projects in Converse County, Wyo. Their operator, Duke Energy Renewables, found 14 golden eagles and 149 other protected birds dead at the two facilities between 2009 and 2013, the US Justice Department said. In November 2013, the company pleaded guilty to violating the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, in what the Justice Department described as the first criminal enforcement of the law for unpermitted bird deaths at wind projects. It was sentenced to pay $1 million in fines, restitution and community service, placed on probation for five years and required to carry out a compliance plan aimed at preventing further bird deaths. An Associated Press investigation earlier that year had identified Top of the World as the deadliest of Duke’s 15 wind facilities for eagles.How the cameras work and what the study foundIdentiFlight is an automatic curtailment system: cameras and software that detect flying objects, classify them and slow or stop turbines when an eagle is at risk of a collision. Using the speed and trajectory of a bird that looks like an eagle, it calculates the time until collision, so a turbine only needs to be slowed down when it has to. The automated curtailment started at Top of the World in August 2018.The researchers used a before-after-control-impact design, comparing a treated site with a control site before and after the device was installed. The treated site was Top of the World. The control site was Campbell Hill, 15 km away, with 66 turbines and no such system. After correcting for carcass detection and scavenger removal rates, the scientists found that fatalities at Top of the World declined 63% between the two periods, while fatalities at Campbell Hill rose 113%. That is where the 82% figure comes from. It is not a single drop. It is the result of setting a fall at one site against a rise at the other. The researchers themselves were cautious. Todd Katzner of the US Geological Survey said the device greatly reduced but did not eliminate eagle collisions, and that it might be combined with other measures, such as avoiding building in high-risk locations.The number in questionIn August 2023, two scientists, Manuela Huso and Dan Dalthorp, published a reanalysis in the Journal of Applied Ecology. They made the point that the initial finding had appeared impressive for its size and its precision and then claimed that it was based on four key mistakes. For instance, in one case, the average number of eagle fatalities for the four years before the system was turned on was compared with the number in one single year afterwards, without accounting for the fact that the number of deaths fluctuates from year to year.After their revisions, they estimated a 50% reduction in the fatality rate, but the confidence interval was wide, ranging from a 159% increase to an 89% reduction. In plain English, the revised data were consistent with anything from a large benefit to no benefit to a rise in eagle deaths. Christopher McClure, the original lead author, responded in the same journal that the reanalysis ignored relevant data and included inappropriate observations. The original authors’ 2022 follow-up, which used data through 2021, put the reduction at 85%, with an uncertainty interval from 12% to 100%.The reanalysis does not say the cameras failed. It argues that a single monitored site over a few years cannot pin down how large the benefit is. The original authors disagree, and the dispute has not been settled. What isn't at issue is the problem itself and the notion behind the answer. Wyoming operators were convicted for killing eagles in wind farms, and a camera system that slows a single turbine just when a bird is near is a viable alternative to shutting down whole complexes. The honest bottom line is that it probably helps; nobody is sure how much, and it works best as one tool among several rather than as a total cure.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2014, Washington State researchers developed an asphalt binder from restaurant fryer oil; they estimated it could cost as little as $200 per ton and reported that road trials were underway
articles.summary: Discover how Washington State researchers are transforming waste cooking oil into a cost-effective and eco-friendly asphalt binder for road construction. Learn about the potential impact on the industry and ongoing road trials.
articles.body: Restaurant fryer oil, usually collected for recycling or discarded after repeated use, offered an unexpected possibility for road construction in 2014. Researchers at Washington State University developed a bio-based asphalt binder using waste cooking oil, aiming to reduce reliance on petroleum while finding a productive use for a common commercial waste product. The team estimated that the alternative binder could cost as little as $200 per ton, compared with the $700 to $800 per ton then quoted for conventional asphalt binder.A road trial was underway at the time. The project explored whether used cooking oil could provide a practical alternative to petroleum-derived binder. Although the early findings attracted interest, the estimated price did not establish the material's final commercial cost, and its long-term performance needed to be assessed under real road conditions.How restaurant oil became an asphalt binderNormal asphalt binder is an oil product which helps keep crushed stones, sand, and other aggregate particles intact. The asphalt binder makes the pavement resistant to mechanical stress and temperature changes. Researchers from Washington State University looked at the possibility of converting waste cooking oil from restaurant deep-fat fryers into a binder which has the characteristics necessary for road building. The research project was headed by Haifang Wen, a civil engineering researcher from Washington State University. The goal of the study was to produce a material which can be applied using normal road paving techniques.Earlier research published in the Journal of Materials in Civil Engineering in 2013 examined waste cooking oil-based bioasphalt as a potential alternative to petroleum-derived binder. The researchers blended the bio-based material with conventional asphalt binders at proportions of 10%, 30% and 60% by weight of the original binder, then tested both the binders and the resulting hot-mix asphalt. The findings showed that adding bioasphalt softened the mixtures, reduced stiffness and resistance to rutting and fatigue cracking, and increased resistance to thermal cracking. The mixtures also passed the minimum tensile strength ratio test for moisture susceptibility. In conclusion, the experiment showed that waste cooking oil can be incorporated into asphalt, but the mix must balance flexibility with resistance to deformation and cracking.The $200 cost estimate and road trialThe financial viability of the project was an important part of the Washington study. In 2014, the university stated that waste cooking oil cost about one-third less than crude oil, while researchers estimated that the recovered-oil binder could cost up to $200 per ton. The study also noted the potential for substantial demand, given the millions of tons of asphalt binder used annually in US road construction. The project progressed from laboratory testing to road trials, with the 2014 report mentioning a test section of at least a quarter-mile. However, the available record does not establish how the test section performed in subsequent years, so the cost estimate should not be treated as proof of long-term commercial success.Can waste oil produce durable roads?The main engineering challenge is balancing flexibility with resistance to deformation. Asphalt must withstand heavy traffic and hot weather without developing ruts, while retaining enough flexibility. A 2016 study in Construction and Building Materials examined bio-oil derived from waste cooking oil as an asphalt modifier. The research indicated that the oil could soften the binder and improve its stress-relaxation properties, potentially helping it resist cracking at low temperatures. However, excessive softening could compromise its resistance to deformation at higher temperatures.The trade-offs suggest that oil quantity, processing method, and the base binder all affect the outcome. More field tests are needed to determine whether the mixture will work under various weather and traffic conditions. The Washington State University research demonstrated the feasibility of using waste oil in road construction. The cost estimate and road tests provided preliminary results, but further investigation is needed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A California homeowner discovered that a utility pole stood on her property for years without her knowledge; the pole company claimed rights on her land
articles.summary: A California homeowner’s discovery that a utility pole stood on her property instead of the neighbouring plot has brought attention to the legal
articles.body: A California homeowner’s discovery that a utility pole stood on her property instead of the neighbouring plot has brought attention to the legal complications that can arise when land boundaries and long-standing infrastructure do not match. The utility company argued that decades of use had given it rights over the land, despite the apparent absence of a formal agreement. The dispute highlights a difficult issue for property owners of whether the passage of time can establish legal rights over privately owned land, and what happens when an intrusion is discovered years after it began.How a utility pole on private property sparked a legal disputeThe case, Graves v. Pacific Gas and Electric Company, was brought by Kimberly A. Graves in the US District Court for the Eastern District of California. According to the court’s order, Graves acquired the property in Stockton in 2009. Both she and Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) believed the pole stood on the neighbouring parcel.That understanding changed in September 2023, when a professional land survey established that the pole was actually within her property boundaries. Graves alleged that neither she nor the previous owners had granted PG&E a lawful easement or other permission to occupy the land. She contacted the company seeking compensation, but PG&E maintained that it had acquired property rights through long-term use.The disagreement became a legal dispute over the company’s continued occupation and the homeowner’s right to control her property.Long-term use can create legal rightsA prescriptive easement is a legal right to use another person’s land that may develop through sustained use, even without a written agreement. As explained by Vokshori Law Group, such rights generally require open and noticeable use, continuity for at least 5 consecutive years, and use that is adverse rather than permitted by the owner.The person claiming the easement must establish these elements through clear and convincing evidence. The length of time alone does not automatically settle the matter. The circumstances surrounding the use, including whether the owner knew about it or gave permission, can be important.An easement also differs from ownership. It may grant someone a limited right to use land without transferring ownership of the land itself. In Graves’s case, PG&E’s position raised the question of whether its long-standing use could establish a valid right to keep the pole in place, even though the property boundary had been misunderstood.The location of the pole affects the owner’s rightsA utility pole can occupy only a small portion of a property, yet its presence may have consequences beyond the ground it covers. The court’s order explained that a permanent physical occupation can restrict an owner’s ability to use the affected area, exclude others and develop the land. It may also reduce the value of the property or complicate a future sale.The distinction matters because a utility’s ownership of equipment does not, by itself, establish an unrestricted right to place it anywhere. As reported by AcreSeal, utility companies commonly own and maintain their poles, while an easement defines their rights to access and use the land beneath them.A deed may identify an existing easement, but the absence of an obvious reference does not automatically resolve every dispute. The relevant documents, the history of the installation and the applicable law all need to be considered.Why the timing of discovery mattersOne of the central difficulties in the Graves case was the time that had passed since the pole was installed. PG&E argued that the homeowner had not owned the property when the original occupation began and that the legal time limit for bringing a claim had expired. The company also disputed whether the delayed discovery rule could apply.The court agreed that Graves’s original complaint did not adequately establish her right to pursue the federal and state compensation claims or explain why the time limits should not apply. However, the order also recognised an important distinction. The proposed amended complaint alleged that neither Graves nor PG&E knew the pole was on her land before the 2023 survey, and that the boundary fencing, maps and utility records had indicated otherwise.The court considered whether these circumstances could bring the case within an exception for physical intrusions that were unknown to both the previous and subsequent owners. It decided that amendment was not necessarily futile and recommended allowing Graves to file an amended complaint. This did not amount to a final ruling that PG&E was liable or that compensation was owed.Evidence can strengthen a property owner’s positionThe dispute demonstrates why property records and reliable evidence can be particularly important when a long-standing structure is found in the wrong place. Vokshori Law Group recommends collecting photographs, maps, witness statements and other documentation when investigating disputes involving long-term use of another person’s land.For a homeowner facing a similar situation, a professional boundary survey can help establish the location of the property line. Reviewing the deed, title records and any recorded easements may clarify whether the utility has a documented right to occupy the land. Records of correspondence with the company can also help establish when the issue was reported and how it was addressed.The July 2026 order in Graves v. PG&E recommended granting the utility’s motion to dismiss the original complaint while allowing Graves an opportunity to amend it. It also addressed her proposed additional claims, including continuing trespass, unjust enrichment and deceptive conduct. The recommendation was therefore a procedural development instead of a final determination of the parties’ rights.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘JD wanted to chat with us real quick’: How Trump’s press secretary was fired mid-interview
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was in the middle of an interview with The Wall Street Journal when President Donald Trump’s senior adviser
articles.body: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was in the middle of an interview with The Wall Street Journal when President Donald Trump’s senior adviser Jason Miller knocked on her office door and told her that Vice President JD Vance wanted to speak with her.“JD wanted to chat with us real quick,” Miller told Zacharia, who was discussing her plans for the role at her West Wing desk shortly before 1 pm on Friday, the Journal reported. The account was also shared on X by WSJ journalist Philip Melanchthon Wegmann.Zacharia left the interview and never returned, with the interruption marking the end of her five-day stint as White House press secretary, the Journal reported. Her departure came just days after she took over the role following Karoline Leavitt’s exit.The development came as Trump was speaking to reporters before departing for Georgia. He said he had advised Zacharia to reconsider taking the job.“I said, ‘Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don’t need this’,” Trump said, adding that he had encouraged her to think again about the role.A difficult first weekZacharia’s short tenure followed a difficult first appearance at the White House briefing room podium on Tuesday. She spoke for about 14 minutes, relied heavily on prepared notes and answered only three questions from reporters representing friendly media outlets.She later told The Wall Street Journal that she had less than 24 hours to prepare for the briefing and received background information only on the morning of the event. She said she had tried to deliver the briefing despite the limited time and information available.“I did everything in my power to effectuate a briefing in the limited time and information I had,” Zacharia told the newspaper hours after her dismissal. “My goal was to serve President Trump and the American people to the best of my ability.”She also said she had difficulty turning down requests because she wanted to work as part of the team, while maintaining that she did not blame the White House for asking her to face reporters so soon.Questions over legal credentialsZacharia’s first week also brought scrutiny over her legal background after Trump described her as an attorney. During her first briefing, she was asked where she had passed the bar exam and said she had done so while living in China.She later acknowledged that she had never passed the bar exam, saying she had practised international transaction law in China with the appropriate credentials.Her explanation drew further questions during an appearance on Fox News’ Hannity, where host Sean Hannity challenged her over why she had not simply said she had never practised law.Despite the short tenure, Zacharia had discussed plans for the press office with the Journal shortly before her dismissal. She said she did not intend to make staffing changes and wanted to keep the team together.“There are no staffing changes that are happening,” she said. “I’m trying to keep everyone cohesive.”Her exit leaves the White House communications role vacant less than three weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.She has become the shortest-serving member of Trump’s White House press team, surpassing communications director Anthony Scaramucci, who left after 10 days during Trump’s first term.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2022, a Norwegian man cycled toward India for nine months, then kept riding until 55,000 km across 46 countries brought him home nearly four years later
articles.summary: Andreas Graf embarked on a bicycle journey from Norway to India, but ended up circumnavigating the globe over three and a half years covering 55,000 km across five continents and facing extreme weather conditions.
articles.body: In April 2022, Andreas Graf set out from his home in Norway on a bicycle, expecting to reach India in about nine months. Instead, the journey led him to travel 55,000 kilometres across five continents and 46 countries, according to the Guardian. What started as a trip towards a single destination turned out to be a circumnavigation that lasted three years and eight months. Graf chose to leave his routine behind to travel mostly under his own power, meet people and spend more time outdoors. A week after leaving home, he was in Sweden, lying in a half-wet sleeping bag while rain poured onto his tent, but he continued through Denmark, Germany and Poland, then south through central Europe, Greece and Turkey. The reason Graf chose cycling was that it allowed him to cover more ground than walking while retaining a slower pace. By the time he reached India, he no longer intended to stop, and the idea of cycling around the world had replaced his original goal.From India through Asia and Oceania to South AmericaAfter India, Graf travelled through Nepal, where he took a break for a month and volunteered on a coffee farm. He then flew over Myanmar, which was closed, before cycling through south-east Asia to Singapore. From that point, he took a ferry to Indonesia and continued by bicycle through Indonesia, Timor-Leste, Australia and New Zealand.His next major leg took him through Chile and Argentina, before he cycled through Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia. At the end of this South American section, he took a final flight to Senegal and cycled north towards Norway, completing the journey on 23 December 2025.Graf met the most brutal conditions in Australia, where he spent two months cycling across the outback during summer, with the exception of one day when the temperature fell below 40°C, he told the Guardian. His loaded bicycle weighed between 52 and 85kg. In addition, he also crossed the Sahara during summer, recording a temperature of 51°C in central Mauritania, Graf said. Strong winds and blowing sand made the crossing particularly difficult and extended it by a month beyond his expectations.Extreme conditions and unexpected kindness during the journeyWhile facing dangers on the road, Graf camped near the Ak-Baital Pass in Tajikistan, at 4,655 metres above sea level, during a storm and woke to clear skies and snow-covered mountains. In northern Chile, he experienced a 7.4-magnitude earthquake; while in Peru, his bicycle along with his tent, mattress and stove broke down and forced him to wait for replacement equipment.After he had cycled almost 10,000 kilometres along the Andes, he crashed while descending a mountain in Colombia after encountering a pothole and an oil spill. The accident broke his wrist, and surgery left him with a titanium plate and eight screws. Along with these hardships, Graf encountered generosity from strangers in rural India, where he was invited for breakfast after a brief, tense encounter. Recalling his experience, Graf told the Guardian: “There was a bunch of guys in front of the tent with knives and machetes and a big flashlight. They were scared; they don’t get a lot of visitors.” In southern Australia, a couple who had seen his photograph on Facebook left him the keys to their house while they had gone away for the weekend.The experience also changed his relationship with work and time. In Australia and New Zealand, he travelled without a phone, often waking with the sun and going to bed with it. His career-focused outlook faded, while his experiences of pollution and extreme temperatures prompted concerns about the future of places he had visited.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pope Leo XIV to be discharged from hospital after successful lung cancer surgery on Saturday
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV is set to leave hospital on Saturday afternoon, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, with doctors declaring him fit for
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV is set to leave hospital on Saturday afternoon, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, with doctors declaring him fit for discharge following blood tests, a chest X-ray and an assessment of his condition, the Vatican said.The 71-year-old pontiff will deliver the traditional noon blessing from a window overlooking St Peter's Square on Sunday, his first public engagement since being admitted to Rome's Gemelli Hospital.Leo underwent surgery on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung after doctors detected a suspected cancerous nodule. The procedure confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.In a statement, his personal physician and surgeon said the pope was “deemed fit for discharge from the hospital” based on Saturday morning's test results and an assessment of his clinical condition.Since the operation, Leo has shown signs of a steady recovery. He held a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, met senior aides and celebrated Mass in a hospital chapel. The Vatican on Friday released the first images of the pope since the surgery, showing him standing at an altar in green vestments.During the Mass, Leo distributed Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said the pope also thanked hospital staff for “the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him”.Doctors are still awaiting test results to establish the cancer's precise molecular and genetic characteristics, whether it has spread beyond the removed lung lobe and whether further treatment will be needed.Leo is scheduled to travel to Latin America from November 6 to 17. The trip would involve a dozen flights and two helicopter journeys, giving him around three weeks to recover after leaving hospital. The Vatican has published the names of journalists accredited to accompany him, indicating that preparations for the visit are continuing.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: At 85 and 82, Ken and Jill Hooper are still restoring Australian bushland; after more than 20 years of conservation work, they have helped protect 970 hectares and bring native wildlife back
articles.summary: At an age when many people settle into a quieter retirement, Ken Hooper, 85, is still reaching for his chainsaw, clearing invasive vegetation and
articles.body: At an age when many people settle into a quieter retirement, Ken Hooper, 85, is still reaching for his chainsaw, clearing invasive vegetation and protecting native wildlife alongside his 82-year-old wife, Jill. For more than two decades, the couple have devoted their time to restoring damaged Australian bushland, demonstrating how conservation can become a lifelong commitment rather than a project confined to working years. Their work on Moona-Bingel, a property near Deniliquin in New South Wales, forms part of a wider movement of older Australians turning retirement into an opportunity to repair the natural environment. As reported by The Guardian in its October 10, 2026, feature, with conservation initiatives supported by Landcare Australia and Australia's broader community landcare network, the Hoopers' efforts reflect a growing interest in protecting habitats, reviving native vegetation and safeguarding biodiversity for future generations.How retirement became a conservation missionKen and Jill's journey into conservation began long before their retirement. In 1992, the couple purchased Wirra-Lo, a 180-hectare property in northern Victoria as part of their dairy farming operation. Rather than allowing the land to remain vulnerable to further environmental damage, they eventually placed it under a conservation covenant and began restoring its natural habitats.Their ambitions, however, extended beyond a single property. The couple later acquired Moona-Bingel in New South Wales, where they committed themselves to rehabilitating a much larger landscape. The conservation agreement covering the 970-hectare property has helped protect the land while the couple work to improve its ecological condition. For a time, they managed both properties, with Ken making frequent journeys between them. In 2023, they sold Wirra-Lo to the Wetland Revival Trust, allowing them to focus their efforts on Moona-Bingel. The work has continued for more than 20 years, involving the removal of invasive weeds, control of feral animals, revegetation and efforts to manage flooding. The scale of the task remains considerable, but the couple's commitment has not diminished with age.Native wildlife is slowly returningThe transformation at Moona-Bingel is becoming visible in the landscape itself. What was once heavily modified agricultural land is developing into a more diverse habitat, with river red gum wetlands, grey box grassy woodlands and sandhill pine woodlands among the ecosystems the couple are working to restore.Their efforts extend beyond planting trees. Managing water supplies to wetlands, controlling invasive species and protecting young vegetation are all essential to helping native habitats recover. Red deer remain a persistent challenge because they can destroy carefully nurtured saplings before they mature.Yet the signs of progress keep appearing. The couple have observed new birdlife, breeding carpet pythons and native plants returning naturally. Their work is also helping protect the ecological character of the Edward River landscape.The NSW Biodiversity Conservation Trust, which supports conservation agreements with private landholders, highlighted the Hoopers' work in a 2024 account of their restoration efforts. The agreement covering 970 hectares was signed in 2018, providing long-term protection for the property and helping ensure that the restored land will not simply return to intensive agricultural use.Why more Australians are turning to conservation after retirementThe Hoopers are part of a broader movement of older Australians finding purpose in environmental work. Landcare Australia's 2026 national survey found that 80% of respondents were aged 55 or older, underlining the significant contribution of older people to community-led conservation.For many, retirement offers something that working life rarely allows: the time to commit to a long-term project whose results may take years to emerge. Conservation also provides a practical way to respond to environmental concerns, from declining biodiversity to damaged waterways and disappearing habitats.The work can be physically demanding, particularly for people managing large properties. Ken continues to use a chainsaw despite osteoarthritis and having undergone two knee replacements, while Jill keeps track of the changes taking place across the land. Their different approaches help them tackle both the demanding physical work and the close observation needed to monitor ecological recovery.A legacy that will outlast themFor the Hoopers, restoring the land is not a task with a neat finishing date. Native forests take years to mature, wetlands require continued attention, and invasive species can undo progress if left unchecked. Protecting the property through a conservation agreement is therefore as important as the work already completed.Their experience also offers a reminder that environmental restoration does not always require grand technological solutions or large institutions acting alone. It can begin with people willing to take responsibility for a piece of damaged land and remain committed long enough to see it change.After more than two decades, Ken and Jill are still looking ahead rather than slowing down. The returning wildlife and recovering vegetation provide evidence that their efforts are making a difference, even as much remains to be done. At Moona-Bingel, retirement has become an ongoing investment in the future, one that may benefit native species and generations of Australians long after the couple can no longer undertake the work themselves.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Another institution being destroyed’: Congress alleges RSS-BJP agenda behind Census 2027 changes
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Congress on Saturday accused the BJP-led Centre of pursuing a political agenda through its expansion of the pool of eligible enumerators
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Congress on Saturday accused the BJP-led Centre of pursuing a political agenda through its expansion of the pool of eligible enumerators for Census 2027. The party cited alleged links to an RSS training camp and a panel on demographic changes.Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh alleged that the developments raise concerns over the census process.The allegations came after the Centre amended the Census Rules, 1990, on Friday, allowing states and Union territories to appoint teachers from aided and unaided private institutions, among others, as census officers."The Modi govt has now expanded the list of eligible enumerators for Census 2027. There is much mischief behind it," Ramesh said in a post on X, alleging that the move could compromise the credibility of the decennial exercise.The Congress leader linked the census notification to an RSS training camp held in Belgaum from July 10 to 12, 2026, which he claimed focused on Census 2027. He also flagged the high-level committee on demographic changes, constituted by the Union home ministry on May 26, 2026, which invited public inputs, including from Indian and foreign organisations, on October 14.“The only thing high level of this committee is the affiliation of its members to the RSS ecosystem. So we know where these inputs will come from,” Ramesh alleged.Calling the expansion a “Rozgar Guarantee Yojana for thousands of RSS/BJP workers”, he claimed it could further undermine the census process.“This will most certainly further contaminate an already subverted Census. Another institution is being destroyed. Like SIR, the Census will also be dangerously doctored,” he said.Also Read| Centre expands Census enumerator pool to include private school teachers, clerksThe notification issued by Registrar General of India Mrityunjay Kumar Narayan specifically includes teachers from government, local authority, aided and unaided private institutions, societies and trusts.The amendment comes amid legal challenges to the deployment of private-school staff for census duties. The Punjab and Haryana high court and the Allahabad high court have granted interim relief in cases concerning the requisitioning of teachers from private institutions.Separately, the National Centre for Promotion of Employment for Disabled People (NCPEDP) has called for accessible and inclusive enumeration in Census 2027, urging clear information on the counting process, accessible self-enumeration facilities and sensitisation of census officials.“The Census 2027 will be the first decennial census since the enactment of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016, which recognises 21 types of disabilities,” the organisation said, according to news agency PTI.The 2027 Census, the eighth since Independence, will be conducted in two phases: house-listing and housing census, followed by population enumeration. Originally scheduled for 2021, the decennial exercise was postponed due to the Covid-19 pandemic, with the Union Cabinet approving Rs 11,718 crore for what is expected to be the country’s largest-ever headcount exercise.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1987, a Queens mother transferred a Ridgewood property but tried to reserve life estates for herself and her daughter; 39 years later, a New York appeals court ruled the daughter never received a valid life estate
articles.summary: A New York woman's attempt to secure her daughter's lifelong rights to a family property has ended in a court ruling nearly four decades after the
articles.body: A New York woman's attempt to secure her daughter's lifelong rights to a family property has ended in a court ruling nearly four decades after the original transfer. In 1987, Mary Mangiaracina transferred a property in Ridgewood, Queens, to another person but included a condition intended to protect her own right, as well as her daughter's, to use the property for life. However, on April 1, a New York appeals court ruled that the daughter had never legally received that right.Mary's daughter, Anna Marie Mangiarcina, went to court in 2023 after the property was sold to new owners. According to the case information published on Justia, Anna Marie Mangiarcina argued that the document signed by her mother in 1987 had given her a lifetime interest in the property. The new owners disagreed.At the centre of the disagreement was a legal arrangement known as a life estate which allows someone to continue using or living in a property for the rest of their life, even when the property belongs to another person.But the judges found a problem with how the arrangement had been made. The court also rejected her separate argument that she had become the owner because of her use of the property over the years.What happened to the Queens property in 1987?The dispute began with a property transfer on September 28, 1987. Mary transferred the Ridgewood property to Joseph C. Murania but attempted to keep lifetime rights for herself and Anna Marie.Mary died in May 2017. More than five years later, on September 9, 2022, the property was sold by a trust created under Murania's will to new owners.The sale was followed by a legal dispute. In January 2023, Anna Marie approached the court, arguing that her mother's agreement still protected her rights.She wanted the court to recognise that she had a life estate in the property. She also sought financial compensation based on that claim. The new owners, however, maintained that she had no such right and asked the court to dismiss her case.Why court rejected the daughter's claimThe judges examined the document signed by Mary in 1987. They found that while she had attempted to reserve lifetime rights for herself and her daughter, the arrangement had not legally created those rights for Anna Marie.The problem was that Anna Marie was not one of the parties to whom the property had been transferred. The court described her as a "stranger to the deed", a legal expression referring to someone who was not a party to the property transfer.Under the legal rule applied in this case, Mary could not give her daughter a valid life estate simply by including her name in the document. The judges said this remained true even if Mary had intended to protect her daughter's interest.Could the daughter claim ownership?Anna Marie also claimed that she had acquired ownership through what is legally called adverse possession. This rule can allow someone to become the legal owner of a property after possessing it for a specified period, based on certain conditions.However, the court found that Anna Marie's earlier use of the property had been permitted. That was important because permission to use a property does not, by itself, establish ownership through adverse possession.The judges found that May 2017, when her mother died, was the earliest possible date from which her claim could be considered.By the time Anna Marie filed her case in January 2023, fewer than six years had passed. The period was shorter than the 10 years required under the rule considered by the court.What the appeals court ruledThe case had initially gone before a Queens County court, which in April 2024 declined to dismiss Anna Marie's claims. The court also considered the request for an early ruling premature, leaving open the possibility of further examination of the evidence. Property owners challenged that decision before a higher court.On April 1, 2026, the appeals court ruled in their favour after finding that Anna Marie had not provided sufficient grounds to show that gathering more evidence could change the outcome.You use AI every day. articles.title: In the 1930s, the West seeded crested wheatgrass to restore damaged land and feed livestock; the introduced grass now dominates roughly 20 million acres
articles.summary: Discover how crested wheatgrass was introduced in the 1930s to restore damaged rangelands and its ongoing influence on native plant diversity across 20 million acres in the American West.
articles.body: Land managers were seeking ways to restore degraded rangelands and provide forage for livestock, so they planted crested wheatgrass in large areas of the American West during the 1930s. The grass is native to the steppes of Russia and Siberia, and was established readily in cold and dry conditions, with an ecological-site assessment from the US Department of Agriculture estimating that about 20 million acres of crested wheatgrass have been planted in the western United States. That figure is an estimate of planting and not a measurement of how many acres are still dominated by the grass today, and it also warns that crested wheatgrass can spread into neighbouring native grasslands and compete with local vegetation.A grass that was chosen for damaged rangelandsCrested wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum) was introduced to the United States in the early 20th century, and the US Forest Service records its first successful establishment in the country between 1907 and 1913, with its use expanding during the 1930s. The grass was practically advantageous for ranchers and land managers, as it tolerates cold and dry conditions, establishes relatively easily, and can remain productive for decades. Those characteristics made it useful in semi-arid regions where native vegetation had been damaged by cultivation, grazing, or other disturbance.The USDA's Agricultural Research Service explains how drought and economic hardship during the 1930s increased pressure to conserve soil and restore damaged rangelands, with New Deal-era conservation programmes expanding seed production and restoration work. Crested wheatgrass was among the introduced perennial grasses that were developed and distributed for these plantings, and the first known range seedings in the Intermountain West took place in 1932 near American Falls, Idaho, and at a USDA sheep experiment station in the state.Why is grass so difficult to replace?The same characteristics that made crested wheatgrass particularly useful for restoration can also create problems when managers want native plant communities to return after some time. The species is a long-lived perennial that has vigorous seedlings and a well-developed root system, and the Forest Service says that it can remain productive for more than 30 years and form stands that are dominated by the introduced grass. Crested wheatgrass greens up earlier in spring than many native bunchgrasses, which allows it to use soil moisture early in the growing season. It produces abundant seed, and established stands can persist even after the original planting objective has changed.The USDA ecological-site assessment identifies crested wheatgrass as a concern in areas where seeded pastures are at the border of native grasslands, since its seeds can dominate the seed bank in invaded areas, while established plants start competing with native grasses. The assessment links these altered plant communities with reduced plant diversity and simpler vegetation structure, but these effects vary by site, and the presence of crested wheatgrass does not mean that every native species will disappear.The acreage estimate needs contextThe estimated 20 million acres is widely cited in USDA ecological-site descriptions, but it traces back to research published in 1981, and should therefore be treated as a historical estimate of how extensively the grass was planted, instead of a current survey of its distribution. The US Forest Service's species review gives a wider range for crested and desert wheatgrass seedings combined, and reports that these grasses were established on 10 million acres and, by some accounts, as much as 26 million acres across North America. The review notes that the two species have very frequently been treated together in planting records, which complicates comparisons between estimates.Restoration goals have changedCrested wheatgrass remains useful as livestock forage and for establishing vegetation on some disturbed sites, and the management challenge only arises where older plantings occupy areas that are now targeted for restoration of native grassland or sagebrush-steppe ecosystems. It would require intensive management to return those sites to native vegetation, especially where the introduced grass has formed persistent stands, and restoration plans may need to control existing vegetation, introduce native seed and monitor the site over several growing seasons.The history of crested wheatgrass creates a practical conflict in rangeland management, since a species that is selected to solve one problem can complicate a later restoration goal. The original plantings addressed problems such as erosion, degraded land and livestock-feed needs, but where conservation priorities now call for greater native plant diversity, land managers must account for the grass's long persistence and competitive growth.You use AI every day. articles.title: Divers find unopened wooden chest on 320-year-old English warship; wreck at high risk of deterioration as more of it emerges
articles.summary: Divers surveying the wreck of a 320-year-old English warship have discovered an unopened wooden chest, exceptionally well-preserved ropes, wooden decks
articles.body: Divers surveying the wreck of a 320-year-old English warship have discovered an unopened wooden chest, exceptionally well-preserved ropes, wooden decks and other objects on the seabed off the Kent coast.According to Historic England, the Northumberland, a 70-gun warship built in Bristol in 1679, sank during the Great Storm of 1703 on the treacherous Goodwin Sands. A survey funded by Historic England revealed that a much larger section of the ship may have survived on the seabed.However, shifting sands, strong currents and marine organisms continue to threaten the wreck. As more of its structure becomes exposed, the fragile site faces an increasing risk of deterioration. The discoveries could help researchers understand shipbuilding and life at sea during the Stuart period.Northumberland wreck reveals wooden chests, preserved ropes and multiple decksThe survey work revealed extensive remains of the Northumberland, including exposed deck planks, the wooden frame of the ship and evidence of multiple wooden decks. Divers also found exceptionally well-preserved organic material, including coils of rope lying on a timber deck. Several wooden chests were discovered, some containing musket balls, while one remained completely sealed with its contents unknown.The survey also confirmed seven iron cannons at the south-eastern end of the wreck site, with another six further north. Other finds included part of a wooden gun carriage, swords, muskets and copper cauldrons. The objects remain in situ on the seabed.How the Northumberland warship sank off the Kent coast in 1703The Northumberland was built in Bristol in 1679 as a Third Rate warship carrying 70 guns. Its construction formed part of Samuel Pepys' efforts to regenerate the English Navy. The ship sank on 26 November 1703 during the Great Storm, which struck the Goodwin Sands off the Kent coast. Three other warships, the Restoration, the Stirling Castle and the Mary, were also lost during the storm. The location of the Mary has yet to be determined. All four ships belonged to Queen Anne's fleet. Queen Anne was the last Stuart monarch and reigned from 1702 to 1714. The Northumberland wreck provides evidence of naval history from this period.Why the Northumberland shipwreck remains at risk despite centuries of preservationThe Northumberland lies across a large area of seabed at a depth of 15 to 20 metres. Although marine deposits and seabed sediments have helped preserve wooden structures and other organic materials, the wreck remains vulnerable to changing conditions. Shifting sands, strong currents and marine boring organisms continue to make the site unstable.More of the ship is becoming exposed, increasing concerns about its deterioration. The wreck was first designated a Protected Wreck Site in 1981 and has been listed on Historic England's Heritage at Risk Register since 2017.Licensee Dan Pascoe regularly monitors its condition as part of ongoing fieldwork supporting the protection of England's 57 Protected Wreck Sites on behalf of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.The Northumberland wreck could bridge the gap between the Mary Rose and HMS VictoryThe extent of the surviving structure makes the Northumberland a potentially important source of information about wooden warships built during the Stuart period. Historic England's Marine Team Leader, Paul Jeffery, said, “The completeness of the Northumberland wreck site is remarkable. Historic England’s diving work is so important to ensure we continue to record what we can of this site. It is a race against time as more of the Northumberland wreck becomes exposed”.Dan Pascoe said the ship has the potential to become one of the best-preserved wooden warships in the UK. Historian Dan Snow, founder and creative director of History Hit, also highlighted its historical significance. He described the wreck as a missing link between the Mary Rose and HMS Victory, saying it could help fill gaps in knowledge about shipbuilding and life at sea during a pivotal period in British history.You use AI every day. articles.title: In the late 1800s, Grand Teton homesteaders planted smooth brome for winter cattle feed; about 4,500 acres remain, forcing a restoration effort that began in 2007
articles.summary: Explore Grand Teton National Park's ongoing restoration efforts that began in 2007 to transform 4,500 acres of smooth brome-dominated fields back to native sagebrush-steppe habitats, supporting wildlife like elk and sage-grouse.
articles.body: About 4,500 acres of former agricultural fields in Grand Teton National Park, Wyoming, are still dominated by non-native grasses, especially smooth brome. Homesteaders planted the grass in the late 1800s for the production of hay for livestock during winter, and more than a century later, the National Park Service is working to restore the fields and bring back native sagebrush-steppe habitat that is used by elk, bison, pronghorn and greater sage-grouse. The restoration programme has been underway since 2007, and the work involves removing established non-native vegetation and reintroducing native grasses, shrubs and wildflowers.The grass remained after the homesteaders leftMany homesteaders who settled in Jackson Hole cleared native sagebrush-steppe vegetation to grow crops and hay, with the short growing season making hay an important agricultural crop, and smooth brome (Bromus inermis) supplying forage that could be harvested and stored for colder months. The former hayfields are concentrated in the Antelope Flats area in the southeastern part of Grand Teton National Park. The original agricultural use has largely disappeared, but the grass is still established across the old fields, and the National Park Service says that these pastures occupy areas that are important to wildlife movement and year-round habitat.Sagebrush-steppe includes native grasses, flowering plants and other vegetation that support wildlife, such as the greater sage-grouse, while elk, bison, pronghorn and moose use the wider ecosystem for food and movement. The park would need to re-establish a diverse native plant community rather than substitute one grass species for another in order to replace the former hayfields.The park's 2007 Elk and Bison Management Plan identified sagebrush habitat restoration as a priority, with vegetation staff beginning the practical restoration process in 2009, according to the park's current account. The work has required repeated treatment and monitoring because smooth brome can regrow after initial removal.Removing the grass is only the first stepRestoration crews use herbicide to clear smooth brome from selected areas, and depending on the site, prescribed burning can also help remove vegetation and reduce the layer of dead plant material. Crews seed the ground with a mixture of native grasses, shrubs and forbs (the botanical term for non-grass flowering plants), once the non-native grass has been controlled. The National Park Service says that fall planting has proven to be more effective than spring planting for sagebrush restoration, with seeds remaining dormant through winter and germinating after snowmelt. Crews also plant nursery-grown native seedlings where appropriate, especially for shrubs and flowering plants that are slower to establish.The process is divided into treatment units so that park biologists can manage the work and monitor results over time. Smooth brome can return from plants that have survived or the seed bank, so removing it once does not guarantee that it will disappear permanently, and follow-up herbicide treatments may be needed in later growing seasons. The park also collects native seed locally so that plants get suited to the region, and monitoring includes documenting plant cover and counting species in established plots. Researchers compare areas that have been restored with healthy sagebrush-steppe communities to assess whether vegetation is moving toward the desired condition.Grand Teton National Park reported in May 2024 that about 1,400 acres were in various stages of restoration, which included areas where native plants had become well established, and the park planned further work at the Slough South and McBride units, including additional seeding and continued monitoring. The park expects the work to continue over many years, with its objective being to establish native sagebrush-steppe vegetation that can sustain itself and support wildlife, even if some smooth brome remains in the landscape.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, Pennsylvania’s 308-acre Crebilly Farm was preserved after five years of local campaigning and a $24 million conservation effort
articles.summary: In 2025, Crebilly Farm in Chester County, Pennsylvania, was preserved as a township park after a $24 million preservation effort, thwarting a proposed housing development by Toll Brothers. Learn about the land's significance, the campaign to save it, and future park plans.
articles.body: Crebilly Farm lies in Westtown Township, Chester County, Pennsylvania, near the junction of Routes 202 and 926. That part of the county has filled steadily with roads, shopping centers, and subdivisions. Natural Lands describes Crebilly Farm as “an oasis of green” in a rapidly developing part of Chester County, with rolling fields, woodlands, and streams. The Robinson family has owned the land since 1937, according to Philadelphia Magazine. In 2016, developer Toll Brothers proposed building 319 homes on the property, and Westtown Township’s Board of Supervisors denied the application. The dispute went to court, and in December 2019 the Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court upheld the denial on most grounds. Today, most of the land is becoming a township park, and the rest is protected by conservation easements.Crebilly’s place in the Battle of Brandywine, September 1777Natural Lands describes the Battle of Brandywine as the first major battle in Britain’s campaign to capture Philadelphia. The same account records that on September 11, 1777, Continental Army General Adam Stephen spotted Hessian troops crossing the property from his lookout at Sandy Hollow. The 2012 Brandywine Battlefield Preservation Plan of Chester County identifies more than 200 historic resources in the battlefield area. Brian O’Leary, executive director of the Chester County Planning Commission, stated in 2016 that Crebilly is located within the study boundary of the plan and that the troops probably marched across the farm.A 319-home plan and five years of volunteer oppositionSupervisor Richard Pomerantz of Westtown stated in the township's release in December 2024 that the other option available for the site was developing 319 houses. According to Natural Lands, “volunteers waged a five-year battle against the sale to Toll Brothers during meetings in the township, on the web, and in court.” The struggle drew enough media attention to become a “David vs. Goliath” story across the area. On October 2, 2017, O. James Lighthizer, then president of the Civil War Trust, which is now the American Battlefield Trust, sent a statement to the Westtown Township Planning Commission urging the preservation of Crebilly Farm because of its significance to the Brandywine Battlefield.The statement cited the National Park Service’s [hyperlink] 2007 Report to Congress on the Historic Preservation of Revolutionary War and War of 1812 Sites in the United States. The report examined 243 battlefields and found that nearly 70% were located in urban areas and that 141 were lost or extremely fragmented, with residential and commercial development identified as the main threats.The 2022 agreement and the November referendumIn 2022, the project moved forward after the developer’s agreement expired and the Robinson family agreed to conservation. On April 4, 2022, Westtown Township’s Board of Supervisors approved an agreement to purchase 208 acres of Crebilly Farm for $20.8 million, according to the township’s referendum FAQ. In early 2022, the township hired Natural Lands to pursue public funding for a price tag of more than $22 million. The November 2022 referendum passed by a two-to-one margin, creating a township open-space fund.How the $24 million for preservation and stewardship was assembledThe $24 million total combines about $7.5 million from Westtown Township’s open-space fund and $16.5 million raised by Natural Lands through public and private grants and gifts from individual donors. The township closed on about 206 acres for $20 million, and the rest of the total covers costs beyond the land purchase, including long-term stewardship. On August 16, 2024, Natural Lands launched the final phase of the Save Crebilly Campaign. By then, more than $20 million had been committed from public funding and private donations, and another $2.5 million was needed to reach the fundraising goal.The campaign announcement also mentions a $2 million challenge from Mt. Cuba Center and an anonymous donor, who will match gifts dollar for dollar. The township's Dec. 9, 2024 statement says that the closing was made with the help of grants made at federal, state, and county level, referendum revenues, Natural Lands' fundraising, and the Delaware River Watershed Protection Fund managed by the Open Space Institute, with a lead grant from the William Penn Foundation.What the land holds today, from park plans to headwater streamsCrebilly was declared preserved forever in May 2025. Conservation easements protect 102 acres of Crebilly Farm, while Westtown Township owns the remaining 206 acres. Natural Lands reports that the township is in the early stages of developing the township-owned land into a passive-use park with walking trails. Three tributaries to Radley Run Creek, totaling 5,600 feet, begin on the property, and the creek drains into Brandywine Creek about one mile away. The 102 acres under easement remain in private hands. The privately held land is divided into four lots, which the Philadelphia Business Journal reported were unsold in March 2025 with an asking price of $11.2 million. Each estate would hold one main house and related structures, and the conservation easements limit development rather than prohibit all building.As of December 2025, local news reports indicated that park development was moving more slowly than anticipated. The 2012 Brandywine Battlefield Preservation Plan calls for better protection of open spaces and historic landscapes in the battlefield area. The plan itself does not protect the property, but the township’s planned park would help preserve the farm within the battlefield study area.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2021, musician Warren Ellis bought and donated 5,000 square metres of land in Sumatra, creating an extension to a wildlife rescue centre for animals that cannot return to the wild
articles.summary: In 2021, musician Warren Ellis donated land to create Ellis Park, a home for rescue animals in Sumatra. This initiative addresses the urgent need for a sanctuary for unreleasable wildlife affected by illegal trade, offering hope and rehabilitation to injured creatures.
articles.body: Wildlife seized from traders in southern Sumatra faces a second challenge after rescue. Many animals recover and return to the forest, but others arrive with injuries or habits that make release impossible, and for years the region has had few places able to keep them. JAAN, the Indonesian wildlife nonprofit whose name stands for Jakarta Animal Aid Network, has worked on that gap, and its website calls the south of Sumatra the main hub for wildlife crime. Ellis Park’s website records that in 2021 Warren Ellis, an Australian musician, bought land next to one of JAAN’s rescue centers and donated it so that animals that could not be released would have a permanent home. The donation was named Ellis Park.JAAN’s Sumatra Wildlife Center opened in 2017 on 7,000 square metresEllis Park’s website states that JAAN has been rescuing and protecting wildlife in Indonesia since 2008. Before JAAN opened a center in the south of Sumatra, most animals seized there were taken to rescue centers in Java and elsewhere, because the area had no rescue center of its own. In 2017, with help from the Bentley Foundation and a private donor, JAAN bought 7,000 square metres of land in southern Sumatra, which became the Sumatra Wildlife Center.From a February 2021 introduction to an April 2021 land giftIn February 2021, Lorinda Jane of Palm Oil Investigations introduced Ellis to Femke den Haas, a co-founder of JAAN, and the three of them met over Zoom during the COVID pandemic. Photographs of Rina, a macaque whose arms had both been amputated, and of a small dog with a broken jaw convinced Ellis to take action. Den Haas shared information about available land next to the center, which Ellis and his family bought and donated to JAAN. The Ellis Park site dates the extension to April 2021, with 5,000 square metres set aside to house wildlife that cannot be released. The park also aims to educate visitors about cruelty to wildlife in the tourism and pet trades. Ellis plans to buy adjoining land in future as a home for elephants and other large wildlife.What a 2024 macaque study explains about animals that cannot be releasedImpacts of illegal trade on socio-emotional and behavioural skills in macaques was published in F1000Research in 2024 by Amapola Rey, Maria Padrell, Miquel Llorente and colleagues. The paper reports that it involved 53 macaques from five species at the Lao Conservation Trust for Wildlife, a former zoo that now operates as a sanctuary.Macaques who had been denied social interaction when young demonstrated less social behavior and exhibited social avoidance as adults, while macaques who were raised by humans demonstrated more aberrant social behavior. The study was conducted in Laos, but some animals at Ellis Park have similar backgrounds. Bon Bon, a pig-tailed macaque, was kept as a pet in Bali and reared in a house without other macaques, and Ellis Park’s profile of him says he lost skills he needs in the wild.Rina, Trinity and a resident list that has passed 100Ellis Park lists more than 100 residents, all of them with a disability and in need of special care. Rina’s profile on the park’s website records that she was rescued in December 2018 from a wildlife trader in Bandung, West Java, who had cut off both of her arms. She is considered a symbol of Ellis Park. Trinity is a gibbon that was illegally kept as a pet for 20 years and has only one arm and one leg left. Brad is a crocodile that lost all his teeth because he was biting the steel bars of his cage. Pearl is a blind macaque that was brought to the sanctuary from a government quarantine facility. There are two sun bears, Henri and Amelia, who were infants at their arrival.Changes in the primate trade in Indonesian wildlife markets over 25 years: Fewer apes and langurs, more macaques, and slow lorises was published in the American Journal of Primatology. It reports that apes and langurs became less common in Indonesian wildlife markets over 25 years, while macaques and slow lorises became more common. The residents of Ellis Park are from both categories. Oscar is a slow loris who suffered severe burns after he came into contact with power lines. The park has noted that slow lorises are captured for sale as pets, with their teeth being pulled out to facilitate handling.Staff, sponsorships and macaque companionsUtami is the veterinarian, Herman is the head keeper, and there are more than five other keepers in the park. Ellis Park’s website says that donations go directly toward the care of the animals. The above-mentioned study suggests that macaques kept by humans with little contact with other macaques may be more prone to anxiety and abnormal behavior, which fits the park’s plan for Bon Bon to keep Rina and Elsa company.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russia rains over 300 drones, missiles on Ukraine, hits 15-plus energy facilities
articles.summary: Russia attacked more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across Ukraine overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on
articles.body: Russia attacked more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities across Ukraine overnight, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday, as Moscow intensified strikes on the country's energy infrastructure ahead of winter. The attacks hit several western and central regions, prompting round-the-clock restoration efforts and raising fears of widespread power cuts.Between 7pm on Friday and 7am on Saturday, Russia launched more than 320 jet-powered and gasoline-powered Shahed drones, loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles against Ukraine's energy sector, cities and communities, Zelenskyy said in a post on X."Yesterday, the Russians carried out one of their largest attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector – more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine. Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved. I thank everyone working practically nonstop to restore power."Zelenskyy said Russia was trying to overwhelm Ukraine's energy reserves and repair capacity by expanding its campaign against critical infrastructure."Russia has expanded its campaign against the energy system and is trying to stretch Ukraine's reserves and repair capacity as thinly as possible," he said.Several regions hit as repair teams work round the clockThe most difficult situation was reported in Lutsk, Rivne, Zhytomyr, Vinnytsia, Shepetivka, Slavuta and Netishyn. Energy facilities in the Kharkiv, Kyiv, Dnipro and other regions were also hit.Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had shot down a significant number of incoming weapons. However, the scale and sustained pace of the attacks were causing serious damage to the country's energy infrastructure."And although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them, the sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences."Russia seeks winter blackout, Zelenskyy warnsThe latest strikes have heightened concerns about Ukraine's ability to maintain electricity and heating supplies as winter approaches. Zelenskyy accused Moscow of seeking to leave millions of Ukrainians without essential services by targeting the energy system."Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this."He called for stronger international action to deter further attacks and welcomed additional support from European partners."It is important that our European partners have already prepared new support packages for Ukraine. I am grateful to them for this. And it is important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening."Zelenskyy criticises US over Russia sanctions legislationZelenskyy also criticised a decision in the United States to disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which he said was intended to increase pressure on Russia and help bring the war to an end."At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end. This Act could have helped enormously – and still can! But it needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters."He argued that easing pressure on Moscow would encourage further aggression rather than bring the conflict closer to a resolution."A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking."Zelenskyy urged Ukraine's partners not to weaken their support and called for continued efforts to end the war."We must not give up ground. We must keep trying to end the war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely. I thank everyone who is truly fighting for peace and helping Ukraine!"You use AI every day. articles.title: Mini Cooper crash: Kerala court rejects bail pleas of 4 accused in accident that killed 3
articles.summary: KOCHI: A Kerala court on Saturday rejected the bail pleas of four accused in the Mini Cooper crash near Kochi that killed three youngsters, prosecution
articles.body: KOCHI: A Kerala court on Saturday rejected the bail pleas of four accused in the Mini Cooper crash near Kochi that killed three youngsters, prosecution sources said.Angamaly Judicial First Class Magistrate Samyuktha M K dismissed the pleas filed by Suhail, Ninav, Ameer and Joel. The detailed order is awaited.Suhail, 19, allegedly driving the car, rammed into a scooter carrying three youngsters on the airport road at Nedumbassery in the early hours of October 11. The victims, including two women, were around 21 years old.A medical examination reportedly found that Suhail’s blood alcohol level was around five times the permissible limit, prompting police to invoke additional charges.Opposing the bail pleas on Friday, the prosecution cited witness statements and CCTV footage as evidence against the accused. It also said blood and urine tests indicated that Suhail was heavily intoxicated.The prosecution argued that the investigation was at a crucial stage and that the two days the accused had spent in police custody were insufficient for the probe. It also contended that the accused came from influential families and their release could hamper the investigation.The defence claimed that the victims had violated traffic rules by travelling on a scooter. Suhail’s lawyer argued that there was no direct eyewitness to the crash and challenged the charge of culpable homicide not amounting to murder. The defence also accused police of sensationalising the incident and said there was no evidence that the car was being driven at high speed.Meanwhile, police, along with officials from the Motor Vehicles Department and Cochin International Airport Ltd (CIAL), inspected the accident site again on Saturday to assess the car’s speed and examine technical aspects of the road, police sources said.Home minister Ramesh Chennithala said the government and the Home Department were taking steps to ensure the accused received the maximum punishment.“All steps are being taken to ensure this. There will be no situation in which the accused can escape the law.
